item.title: Who is Karen Attiah? Arbitrator orders Washington Post to rehire columnist wrongfully fired over Charlie Kirk posts
item.description: Washington Post columnist Karen Attiah has been ordered to be reinstated with back pay after an arbitrator ruled she was wrongfully fired over social media posts following Charlie Kirk’s assassination. The Post had cited violations of its social media policy.
item.dc:creator: Prabhakar Jha
item.content:encoded: Karen Attiah, a former opinion columnist at The Washington Post, has been ordered to be reinstated with back pay after a private arbitrator ruled that the newspaper wrongfully terminated her over social media posts following the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, New York Times reported.Arbitrator Sarah Miller Espinosa found that The Washington Post "did not have good and sufficient cause" to fire Attiah and had violated its labour agreement, according to the decision made public Monday."The Washington Post failed to establish the grievant engaged in gross misconduct," Espinosa wrote, according to a copy of the ruling shared with The New York Times by Attiah's lawyers.Who is Karen Attiah?Attiah is an opinion journalist who worked at The Washington Post and wrote about politics, race, culture and international affairs.She was among the journalists whose employment came under scrutiny after comments made in the aftermath of Kirk's assassination in September 2025.Attiah posted comments on Bluesky on September 10, the day Kirk was shot. One of her posts discussed the reaction to Kirk's death and his previous comments about Black women.The Washington Post subsequently fired her, saying her social media posts had harmed "the integrity" of the organisation and violated its social media policy.Attiah disputed that reasoning and maintained that her posts were within the scope of her work as an opinion columnist. Why was Attiah fired?The dispute centred on Attiah's social media activity following Kirk's assassination.According to Axios, The Post's head of human resources, Wayne Connell, told Attiah in her termination letter that her posts "harm the integrity of our organization" and could potentially endanger the physical safety of staff.The newspaper also argued that the posts violated its standards requiring employees to use social media with civility and respect.Attiah, however, argued that commenting on political violence was part of her role as an opinion journalist. During an arbitration hearing in June, she defended her posts and said they were part of her work at The Post.What did the arbitrator say?The arbitrator rejected The Post's justification for terminating Attiah.Espinosa concluded that the newspaper had failed to establish that Attiah's conduct amounted to "gross misconduct" and found that the termination violated the labour agreement.She ordered The Post to reinstate Attiah and compensate her with back pay and lost benefits, according to Reuters.The Washington Post News Guild said the decision vindicated its fight to protect journalists' rights. The newspaper's spokesperson said The Post respects the arbitration process and declined to comment further.Will Karen Attiah return to The Washington Post?Attiah said she was "willing to go back" to The Post and described the ruling as confirmation that she had been doing her job as an opinion writer."This decision confirms what we've said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion writer, and this was wrongful termination," she said, according to The New York Times.She also said she hoped the decision would send a message to journalists and media organisations about the importance of protecting freedom of expression.The case is significant because the ruling comes amid wider debate over journalists' social media activity, newsroom policies and free speech protections.
